info.name: Events & Media API
info.description:
# Events & Media API

Every endpoint the API serves, in an order that runs top to bottom: the sign-up
requests capture the one-time code and the tokens into collection variables,
and everything after them uses those.

**Run it with the Collection Runner** and it exercises the whole surface —
sign-up, verification, the welcome perk, all the page content, the event builder
end to end, a vendor application, sign-in, sign-out, a password reset, and
thirteen deliberate failures.

The builder folder is the one worth reading. It prices a package, submits it,
reloads it by reference, and pins down the two rules the contract rests on:
**no price is accepted from the client**, and a **stale running total is an
error rather than a wrong quote**.

## Before the first run

1. Start the stack from the repository root: `docker compose up`.
2. Select the **Events & Media — local** environment (or just leave `baseUrl`
   at `http://localhost:4000`).

Nothing else needs setting. `01 · Sign up` generates a fresh email address
every run, so re-running never collides with the account it made last time.

## Rate limits

One run fits inside the API's budgets. **A second run within the minute does
not** — the password endpoints allow 12 calls a minute per address and a run
spends 10 of them. The builder folder is well inside its own budget: pricing a
package is not a write, so it allows 120 calls a minute.

To re-run freely, turn the limiter off. In `docker-compose.yml` under
`services.api.environment` the line is already there, commented out:

```yaml
RATE_LIMIT_DISABLED: "true"
```

Then `docker compose up -d api`. The API logs a warning at startup while it is
off, and the switch cannot take effect when `NODE_ENV=production`.

Leave it alone and the collection still passes — just wait a minute between
runs. The collection logs a warning to the Postman console whenever a 429
arrives on a request that did not expect one, so that failure is easy to
recognise.

## Development codes

There is no mail provider wired up, so `EXPOSE_DEV_CODES=true` — the
development default — echoes the one-time code back as `devCode` and the reset
token as `devToken`. That is what lets these requests chain. It is forced off
when `NODE_ENV=production`, so the auth folders cannot run end to end against a
production API.

## Shape of every response

Success is always `{ "data": … }`. Failure is always
`{ "error": { "code", "message", "details"? } }`, and `message` is written to
be shown to a user as-is. A collection-level test asserts that envelope on
every single response, so each request below only checks what is specific to
it.

## Auth

The collection sends `Authorization: Bearer {{accessToken}}` by default.
Requests that must be anonymous — the health checks, and the "perk without a
token" case — override it with **No Auth**.

Two rules are worth knowing before reading the auth folders, and both have
tests that pin them down:

- **A password alone is never a session.** `signup` and `signin` both end at a
  one-time code; only `otp/verify` mints tokens.
- **Nothing reveals whether an address is registered.** Signing up with an
  address already on file answers exactly like signing in with it. Signing in
  with an unknown address answers byte for byte like a wrong password, and
  takes the same time. `password/forgot` always answers 202.

exec: // Runs after every request in the collection.
// Every response is either { data } or { error }, so asserting
// the envelope once here keeps each request's own tests to what
// A 204 carries no body by design (the analytics beacon), so there is no
// envelope to assert. Everything else must have one.
pm.test("Response is a JSON envelope", function () {
pm.expect(hasData || hasError, "body has neither data nor error").to.be.true;
pm.expect(body.error.code, "an error needs a machine-readable code").to.be.a("string");
pm.expect(body.error.message, "an error needs a message fit to show a user").to.be.a("string");
// A 5xx is never an expected outcome here - not even in the
// error-cases folder, which is all 4xx by design. The one
// exception would be /health/ready reporting 503, and that is a
// A 429 on a request that does not expect one almost always means
// the run tripped the per-address ceiling rather than anything
// being wrong with the request. Say so, loudly.
" - if this request did not expect it, the run hit the API's rate limit. " +
"Set RATE_LIMIT_DISABLED=true on the API (see the collection description)."

`/health` answers as long as the process is up. `/health/ready` also checks
the database and answers **503** if it is unreachable — that is the one
Compose and a load balancer should watch.

item.name: 01 · Auth — create an account
item.description:
The sign-up half of the flow, in order.

**A password alone is never a session.** `signup` and `signin` both end at
a one-time code; only `otp/verify` mints tokens.

With no mail provider wired up, `EXPOSE_DEV_CODES=true` (the development
default) echoes the code back as `devCode`, which is what lets these
requests chain. It is forced off when `NODE_ENV=production`, so this folder
only runs end to end against a development API.

request.description:
Creates the account and issues a one-time code. Answers **201** with
a challenge, *not* a session.

A fresh email address is generated before the request so the
collection can be re-run without colliding with the account it made
last time.

Note what this does **not** do: signing up with an address already
on file answers exactly like signing in with it — a code goes to
that inbox and only whoever reads it can proceed. See
*08 · Error cases* for the requests that pin that behaviour down.

request.description:
Expected to fail with **401**. The JWT itself still verifies — its
signature and expiry are fine — but the `sessions` row it names was
revoked by the rotation, and that row is what decides. This is why
refresh tokens are backed by a table at all: a JWT alone cannot be
revoked.

item.name: 07 · Auth — sign out
item.description:
Signing out revokes the `sessions` row the refresh token names, which is
the only thing that can actually invalidate a token this API has already
handed out.

request.description:
Takes either credential: a refresh token names one session to close,
and an access token alone closes every session on the account.
Sending neither is the one case that cannot do anything, and answers
**400**.

Answers the same whether or not the session was still live — signing
out twice is not an error worth reporting.

Expected to fail with **401**. The refresh token is still a valid,
unexpired JWT — but its session row is revoked, and the row is what
decides.

item.name: 08 · Password reset
item.description:
**Nothing here reveals whether an address is registered.** `forgot` always
answers 202; the only difference between a known and an unknown address is
whether a token was actually created, which the caller cannot see (outside
development, where `devToken` is echoed so the flow is testable).

Completing a reset ends every session on the account: if the reset was
needed because someone else had the old password, their session goes with
it.

request.description:
**202** Accepted. Asking for a second link invalidates the first, so
a forwarded old email cannot be used later.

The token is stored only as a SHA-256 digest, so a leaked database
cannot be used to complete the reset.

item.name: 09 · Error cases
item.description:
Every request in this folder is **expected to fail**, and each one pins down
a decision rather than just poking at the API.

Failure is always `{ "error": { "code", "message", "details"? } }`.
`message` is written to be shown to a user as-is. `details` carries either a
list of field errors — `[{ "field", "message" }]`, which the sign-in form
paints onto its inputs — or an object such as
`{ "retryAfterSeconds": 29 }`.

Run this folder after *07*: two of the requests rely on the live one-time
code challenge that *07* left behind.

item.name: Sign up with an invalid form

request.description:
**422** with one message per field, which is the shape the sign-in
form paints onto its inputs. One field can raise several issues
(too short *and* missing a digit), so only the first survives — the
form shows one message per input.

exec: pm.test("Reports every bad field, once each", function () {
pm.test("Every message is fit to show a user", function () {
